title: Regenerative agriculture

definition.text: An approach to farming that aims to restore rather than just sustain, rebuilding topsoil, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

facts.text: It is not one practice but a combination of sustainable agriculture techniques, such as recycling farm waste and adding compost.
The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s.
A 2020 review of 229 articles and 25 websites found no legal or broadly accepted definition; some definitions name practices, others outcomes.
Its four most consistent principles are improving soil health, optimising resource use, easing climate change and improving water quality and availability.
An estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost since tillage-based farming began.

A 2023 review found reduced tillage, cover crops, crop–livestock integration and agroforestry can improve soil carbon or yields in some conditions, but evidence on benefits and profitability is limited.
Some scientists call proponents' climate claims exaggerated and unsupported.

contested_note: Scientists dispute claims that regenerative practices, especially grazing, can store enough carbon to counter climate change.

title: Holistic planned grazing

definition.text: Moving livestock herds constantly between fields to imitate how wild herds graze.

facts.text: Supporters say trampling restores soil, stimulates regrowth and raises soil carbon and water infiltration.
A meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it did no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass.
Allan Savory claimed in a TED talk that it could bring carbon dioxide back to pre-industrial levels in 40 years; critics reject this.

contested_note: Evidence on its carbon benefits is mixed, and critics reject the claim that it can reverse climate change.

definition.text: A strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from the effects of nearby land use.

facts.text: Buffers catch sediment, nutrients and pesticides in runoff before they reach the water.
They counter eutrophication downstream and stabilise banks against erosion.
They provide habitat and wildlife corridors in farming areas.
A nine-year University of Georgia study found buffers removed at least 60% of nitrogen and 65% of phosphorus from fertilizer runoff.
Buffers can raise land value and allow profitable crops such as black walnut and hazelnut.
Programmes such as the US Conservation Reserve Program pay farmers to make up for taking buffer land out of production.
A 2017 study found little ability to stop glyphosate leaching to streams.

definition.text: The usual three-zone layout of a riparian buffer, from stream-side trees to outer grass strips.

facts.text: The zone next to the water holds fast-growing native trees that shade the stream and stabilise the bank.
The middle zone of native shrubs gives wildlife habitat and absorbs what the outer zone misses.
The outer grass zone is the first defence, slowing runoff and absorbing contaminants.
A typical recommended width is 50 feet (15 m) on each side of the stream.

definition.text: A riparian buffer whose width follows local groundwater flow instead of a fixed distance.

facts.text: Groundwater enters streams at hotspots that matter disproportionately for temperature, acidity and nutrient retention.
Soil wetness maps from elevation models show where buffers should be wider.
Designing by hydrology rather than fixed width can save money in forestry.
